subject: English
topic: Spotting Errors — Agreement, Preposition, Tense and Idiom Rules (W12 B1)

questions.stem: Find the error: (A) A number of students / (B) was absent / (C) yesterday due to / (D) the heavy rains
questions.explanation: B is correct. 'A number of + plural noun' takes a PLURAL verb. 'A number of students' = several students → plural → 'WERE absent'. Contrast: 'The number of students was...' (here 'the number' is the subject = singular). Rule: A number of = many/several (plural); The number of = the count (singular). Trap: students often use 'was' because 'a number' seems singular — but the noun phrase acts like 'many'.

questions.stem: Find the error: (A) She suggested me / (B) to apply for the job / (C) before the deadline / (D) No error
questions.explanation: A is correct. The verb SUGGEST does not take a direct personal object followed by an infinitive. 'Suggested me to apply' is wrong. Correct patterns: 'She suggested THAT I apply' or 'She suggested applying'. Compare: 'advised me TO apply' is correct (ADVISE takes person + infinitive). Trap: students write 'suggested me to' on the analogy of 'told me to', 'asked me to', 'advised me to' — but 'suggest' does not follow this pattern.

questions.stem: Find the error: (A) If I / (B) will go there, / (C) I will meet him / (D) for sure
questions.explanation: B is correct. In conditional sentences with 'if', the if-clause uses Simple Present (not future). Correct: 'If I GO there, I will meet him.' The future meaning is implied by context, but the grammar rule demands Simple Present in the if-clause. Same for: when/after/before/until/as soon as + Simple Present (not future). Trap: 'If I will go' sounds natural to Hindi-medium speakers (Hindi allows future in the if-clause) but is wrong in English.

questions.stem: Find the error: (A) She is senior / (B) than me / (C) in this organisation / (D) No error
questions.explanation: B is correct. Latin-origin comparatives (senior, junior, superior, inferior, major, minor, prior, anterior, posterior) take the preposition TO, not 'than'. Correct: 'She is senior TO me.' SSC favourite rule: senior/junior/superior/inferior/major/minor + TO (never 'than'). Trap: students use 'than' by analogy with 'older than', 'taller than' — but these native-English comparatives use 'than'; Latin-origin ones use 'to'.

questions.stem: Find the error: (A) He has been working / (B) in this company / (C) since five years / (D) No error
questions.explanation: C is correct. SINCE = used with a point in time (since 2020, since Monday, since morning). FOR = used with a period/duration of time (for five years, for two hours). '5 years' is a DURATION, so it takes 'FOR'. Correct: 'He has been working in this company FOR five years.' Trap: since/for confusion is very common; students mistakenly use 'since' for durations in translations from Hindi (Hindi uses 'se' for both).

questions.stem: Find the error: (A) He is / (B) the taller / (C) of the three / (D) brothers
questions.explanation: B is correct. Rule: Comparative degree ('taller', '-er') is used when comparing TWO things; Superlative ('tallest', '-est') is used when comparing THREE or more. Here we're comparing among three brothers → use 'tallest'. Correct: 'He is the TALLEST of the three brothers.' Trap: students use 'taller' because it sounds more modest — but the grammatical rule demands superlative when the comparison set has 3+ members.

questions.stem: Find the error: (A) Being a rainy day, / (B) we decided / (C) to stay / (D) indoors
questions.explanation: A is correct. DANGLING MODIFIER: 'Being a rainy day' is a participial phrase that should modify the subject of the main clause. The main subject is 'we' — but 'we' cannot be a rainy day. The phrase dangles without a proper subject. Correct: 'As it was a rainy day, we decided to stay indoors.' Trap: the sentence sounds natural but is grammatically incorrect — the implied subject of 'Being a rainy day' must match 'we', which is logically impossible.

questions.stem: Find the error: (A) Scarcely had I / (B) entered the room / (C) when the phone / (D) ringed
questions.explanation: D is correct. The verb 'ring' has an irregular past tense: ring → rang → rung. 'Ringed' is incorrect (as if 'ring' were a regular verb). Correct: 'the phone RANG'. Note: 'scarcely...when' is the correct idiomatic construction (not 'scarcely...than') — so A,B,C are all correct. Trap: 'scarcely...when' is sometimes confused with 'no sooner...than' — but 'scarcely/hardly/barely' always take 'when/before', not 'than'.

questions.stem: Find the error: (A) Had I known / (B) the answer, / (C) I would / (D) answered it
questions.explanation: D is correct. Third conditional structure: 'If/Had + Past Perfect, would have + Past Participle.' Result clause needs 'WOULD HAVE answered' — not just 'would answered'. Correct: 'I would HAVE answered it.' The inverted form 'Had I known' = 'If I had known' (both correct). Trap: 'would answered' is a common error where students use the base form after 'would' (correct in 2nd conditional: 'I would answer'), but in 3rd conditional the auxiliary 'have' is required.

questions.stem: Find the error: (A) The committee of doctors / (B) have decided / (C) to go on strike / (D) from Monday
questions.explanation: B is correct. 'The committee' = a collective noun. When a collective noun acts as a single body taking a unified decision, it takes a SINGULAR verb. 'The committee... have decided' → should be 'HAS decided' (the committee as a single body made one decision). Correct: 'The committee of doctors HAS decided.' Contrast: if the committee is divided and members act individually, plural verb is used — but 'decided to go on strike' implies collective unified action. Trap: 'doctors' is plural, tempting students to use 'have'; but the grammatical subject is 'the committee' (singular).
